title: Knoist un sine dre Sühne
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 138. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 138 is one of the shortest and oddest pieces in the whole collection: barely a page, in Low German, about a man named Knoist whose three sons are blind, lame, and stark naked, and what they manage to do about a hare and a leaky boat. It reads more like a fragment of nonsense verse than a story with a moral, ending in a rhymed couplet about the man who escapes the holy water. Its charge is in the absurd particulars, not a plot to follow.

sentences.t: Twisken Werrel un Soist, do wuhnde ’n Mann, un de hede Knoist, de hadde dre Sühne, de eene was blind, de annre was lahm un de dridde was splenternaket.
sentences.l: Between Werrel and Soist, there dwelt a man, and he was called Knoist, he had three sons: the one was blind, the other was lame, and the third was stark-naked.
sentences.i: Between Werrel and Soist there once lived a man, and his name was Knoist; he had three sons — one was blind, the second lame, and the third stark naked.
sentences.n: The whole tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), in the Westphalian speech of the region it names — expect it in every line. Here: twisken = zwischen, do = da, wuhnde = wohnte, de = der/die, hede = hieß, dre = drei, Sühne = Söhne, eene = (der) eine, annre = andere, dridde = dritte. Two spellings to hold on to from the start: was is war, “was” (the dialect word for “what” is wat), and ’n is the clipped ein, “a” — not ihn. Werrel and Soist are real Westphalian places (Wörl and Soest), so the tale opens like a chronicle and then abandons sense altogether.

sentences.t: Do giengen se mol öwer Feld, do sehen se eenen Hasen.
sentences.l: Then went they once over field, then saw they a hare.
sentences.i: One day they went out across the fields, and there they saw a hare.
sentences.n: giengen is the 1857 spelling of gingen. mol = mal, “once”; öwer = über. sehen here is not the infinitive but the past sahen, “saw” — the dialect levels the two. “öwer Feld gohn” is to go out across country.

sentences.t: De blinne de schöt en, de lahme de fienk en, de nackede de stack en in de Tasken.
sentences.l: The blind one, he shot it, the lame one, he caught it, the naked one, he stuck it in his pocket.
sentences.i: The blind one shot it, the lame one caught it, and the naked one stuck it in his pocket.
sentences.n: The joke is three impossibilities in a row: a blind marksman, a lame runner, a naked man with a pocket. en here is ihn, “him, it” (the hare) — the same two letters elsewhere are en = ein, “a.” blinne = Blinde, schöt = schoß, fienk = fing, nackede = Nackte, stack = steckte (here transitive, stuck it in), Tasken = Tasche. The doubled “De blinne de …” — subject, then a resuming der — is ordinary spoken emphasis in this dialect and recurs through the tale.

sentences.t: Do käimen se für en groot allmächtig Waater, do wuren dre Schippe uppe, dat eene dat rann, dat annre dat sank, dat dridde, do was keen Buoden inne.
sentences.l: Then came they before a great almighty water, there were three ships upon it, the one it ran, the other it sank, the third, there was no bottom in it.
sentences.i: Then they came before a great, mighty water, and three ships were afloat on it: the one ran, the other sank, and in the third there was no bottom at all.
sentences.n: für here is vor, “before, in front of,” not High German für “for.” Schippe is Schiffe, ships — not Schippe, a shovel. wuren = wurden/waren; uppe = (oben) darauf, afloat on it; Buoden = Boden; inne = darin. allmächtig, literally “almighty,” is used all through this tale as a plain intensifier — mighty, enormous. What rann means of a boat is arguable: most likely it ran, that is leaked, though it could simply be that it raced along.

sentences.t: Wo keen Buoden inne was, do giengen se olle dre inne.
sentences.l: Where no bottom in it was, there went they all three in.
sentences.i: The one with no bottom in it — into that one the three of them got.
sentences.n: olle here is alle, “all” (olle dre = alle drei), not olle = alte, “old.” The two inne do different work: the first is “in it,” the second is the separated prefix of ingohn, hineingehen, to go in. The nonsense keeps its own logic — they board the one boat that cannot possibly float.

sentences.t: Do käimen se an eenen allmächtig grooten Walle (Wald), do was en groot allmächtig Boom inne, in den Boom was eene allmächtig groote Capelle,
sentences.l: Then came they to an almighty great Walle (wood), there was a great almighty tree in it, in the tree was an almighty great chapel,
sentences.i: Then they came to a mighty great wood, and in it stood a great mighty tree, and in the tree was a mighty great chapel,
sentences.n: (Wald) is the Grimms’ own parenthesis, printed in the 1857 text to explain the dialect Walle to their readers — every round bracket in this tale is theirs, not an editor’s. Where they gloss a dialect word this way, the literal line keeps the dialect word and puts their gloss, translated, in the brackets. Boom = Baum, Capelle = Kapelle. The impossibilities now nest one inside the other: a chapel inside a tree inside a wood.

sentences.t: in de Capelle was een hageböcken Köster un en bußboomen Pastoer, de deelden dat Wiggewaater mit Knuppeln uit.
sentences.l: in the chapel was a hornbeam sexton and a boxwood parson, who dealt the holy water out with cudgels.
sentences.i: and in the chapel were a sexton of hornbeam and a parson of boxwood, who dealt out the holy water with cudgels.
sentences.n: hageböcken is hagebüchen, “of hornbeam,” and bußboomen is buchsbaumen, “of boxwood” — both proverbially hard woods, and hagebüchen had already come to mean coarse, rough, brutal. Köster = Küster (sexton), Pastoer = Pastor, Wiggewaater = Weihwasser (holy water), Knuppeln = Knüppeln (cudgels). “uitdeelen” = austeilen, to deal out, with its prefix uit waiting at the end of the clause.

sentences.t:
Sielig is de Mann,
de den Wiggewaater entlaupen kann.
sentences.l:
Blessed is the man,
who the holy water can escape.
sentences.i:
Blessed is the man
who can get away from the holy water.
sentences.n: The two-line proverb that closes the tale, and the point of all the nonsense before it: after a hornbeam sexton and a boxwood parson laying about them with cudgels, the blessing belongs to whoever can run from the holy water. The German rhymes Mann with kann. sielig = selig, blessed; entlaupen = entlaufen, to run away from, taking its object in the dative (den Wiggewaater). The cadence “Selig ist der Mann, der …” is the cadence of the psalms and the Beatitudes, which is what makes it a joke.

glossary.den: Low German: den — the (masc. sg.); this dialect uses den where High German has the dative dem (“in den Boom” = in dem Baum; “den Wiggewaater entlaupen” = dem Weihwasser entlaufen)
glossary.en: Low German: ihn — him, it (here the hare); the same spelling is also en = ein, ‘a’
glossary.für: Low German: vor — before, in front of (‘für en Waater’ = vor ein Wasser)
glossary.hasen: der Hase — hare (acc. sg. Hasen; here a single hare, not the plural)
glossary.n: Low German: ’n — ein, a (‘’n Mann’ = ein Mann)
glossary.olle: Low German: alle — all (‘olle dre’ = alle drei); elsewhere olle = alte, old
glossary.schippe: Low German: Schiffe — ships (pl. of Schipp = Schiff); not die Schippe, a shovel
glossary.sehen: Low German: sahen — saw (sehen, 3rd pl. past)
glossary.stack: stecken — stuck, put (3rd sg. past, transitive; ‘stack en in de Tasken’ = steckte ihn in die Tasche)
glossary.was: Low German: war — was (sein, 3rd sg. past; the dialect word for ‘what’ is wat)
